replies:
Good — final round prep, focused and practical. One next step after this: tell me whether your final is virtual or on-site and who (titles) you’ll meet, and I’ll tailor the mock.

Below is a tight, use-in-interview prep plan plus scripts and practice prompts for an analyst final at Lincoln International (M&A-focused). I assumed a final-round that mixes technical accounting/valuation questions and behavioral fit questions; if your posting says otherwise I’ll update.
1) Two-sentence “Why Lincoln International” (say this in the room)
- Example: “I want to be at Lincoln because of its focus on middle-market M&A and high transaction volume across industry-specialist teams — that’s where I’ll get exposure to full-deal execution and the technical modeling work I enjoy. The firm’s emphasis on collaborative teams and client continuity matches how I like to develop deep sector knowledge and long-term client relationships.”

2) 60-second “Tell me about yourself” (analyst version — use our facts to fill brackets)
- Script: “[Your name]. I’m an analyst with [X months/years] of experience in [investment banking / corporate finance / private equity / accounting], where I’ve focused on financial modeling, valuation and deal execution. Most recently at [employer], I built a 3-statement model and led valuation analyses for a [size]-million [sector] sell-side process that helped the team refine price expectations and prepared materials used in the buyer outreach. I like hands-on modeling, working with clients to clarify value drivers and learning sector specifics quickly — which is why I’m excited for analyst work on live M&A at Lincoln.”
- How to personalize: drop one concrete result (percent improvement, $ value, or number of models/deals).
3) Three stories to have ready (STAR, each 45–75 seconds; include a numeric result)
- Team win: Situation, your role, actions you took (modeling, coordinating, tightening assumptions), and result (deal launched, management praise, saved hours). Example metric: “reduced model clean-up time by 30%” or “helped produce CIM that accelerated buyer interest, leading to 10 NDA requests.”
- Hard problem: Complex accounting or a tight deadline. Emphasize how you prioritized, simplified assumptions for the model, and validated numbers with management or auditors. Result: on-time deliverable used in negotiation or senior review.
- Failure / learning: A model error or missed assumption. Say what happened, how you found it, how you fixed compensation/communication, and the process change you implemented (checklist, peer review) and outcome (zero repeat errors).
- Practice prompt: Give each story a single crisp metric and what you learned.
4) Core technical topics to prep (short drills)
- Accounting: walk through how a change in revenue or depreciation flows through the 3 statements; what happens to cash if you increase AR; basics of working capital. Practice: “If revenue increases with a 10% net margin, how does cash change in year 1?”
- Valuation: DCF basics (unlevered free cash flow → enterprise value → equity value), WACC components, terminal value methods (Gordon vs exit multiple) and common sensitivity table setup. Practice: “How do you calculate unlevered FCF from EBIT?”
- Transaction mechanics / M&A: basic purchase price allocations, sources & uses, and simple accretion/dilution logic for a deal with stock and cash consideration. Practice: “Why might a buyer prefer an asset sale vs. stock sale?”
5) Five likely technical questions and how to answer them
- “Walk me through a DCF.” — 6–8 step concise walkthrough: project revenue → margins → NOPAT → add back D&A → change in WC & capex → get unlevered FCF → discount with WACC → derive EV → subtract net debt → equity value → per-share. Mention sensitivity table.
- “How does depreciation affect the 3 statements?” — Income statement: D&A reduces operating income and taxes; Cash flow: add-back on CFO; Balance sheet: accum. depreciation reduces book value of PPE.
- “What is working capital and why does it matter?” — Explain components, why cash conversion cycle matters for free cash flow and deal financing.
- “How do you value a company with negative cash flow?” — Use market comps, precedent transactions, and justify terminal assumptions; explain when an option-based or sum-of-the-parts approach is appropriate.
- “Walk me through an LBO at a high level.” — Sources & uses, financing structure, key returns drivers: entry multiple, exit multiple, leverage, margin expansion, and EBITDA growth.
6) Behavioral/fit questions to prep and short answers
- “Why investment banking / M&A?” — One-sentence motivation + one-sentence example demonstrating curiosity for deals and hard financial work.
- “Tell me about a time you had conflict with a teammate.” — Use STAR, emphasize resolution and what you changed.
- “Where do you see yourself in 3 years?” — Focus on technical competence, leading parts of a deal process, and industry expertise.
7) Two smart questions to ask them (use at end)
- “What are the most common career paths your analysts take after two to three years here?” (shows career thinking)
- “What kind of modeling or client exposure can an analyst expect to own on a typical live sell-side process?” (shows interest in work content)
8) Quick checklist the day before / morning of
- Confirm time, time zone, link/address and interviewers (ask recruiter if not given).
- Have one printed resume and one clean laptop copy; open a recent model and one deal summary to reference.
- Bring a short list of 3 industry facts about the sector you expect (revenue drivers, multiples, recent comparable deal).
- For virtual: test camera, mic, background, and screen-sharing. Use wired internet.
9) Mock practice option (how we’ll run it)
- I’ll ask: one behavioral opener (“tell me about yourself”), two technical drills (one accounting flow question, one DCF question), one tough case prompt (simple 5-minute modeling problem), then two behavioral follow-ups. After you answer each, I’ll score structure, evidence, specificity and give one concrete fix. Say “mock me now” to start.

10) Quick scoring rubric I’ll use in mock
- Structure: clear opening, middle (actions), result/lesson.
- Evidence: one specific metric or example.
- Specificity: names, numbers, timeline, your exact role.
- If any weak spot: I’ll give one edit that makes the answer 30–60 seconds tighter.
Note on pay: I don’t have verified pay or compensation figures unless a posting or tool returns them; I won’t state numbers otherwise.

Next step: is your final virtual or in person, and who (titles) will you meet?
items.note: Reply includes a concrete, structured prep plan for a final-round analyst interview, contains no disallowed phrases or invented firm facts, and directly asks the requested next-step question.
